overview:
Portugal occupies the western rim of the Iberian Peninsula, the last mainland in Europe before the open Atlantic. It shares a border with only one country, Spain, and covers about as much ground as Indiana. Two Atlantic island groups, the volcanic Azores and subtropical Madeira, belong to Portugal as well.

About 10 million people live here and speak Portuguese, a language sailors and settlers carried around the globe; more than 250 million people now speak it, in Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, and beyond. Lisbon, the capital, climbs steep hills above the Tagus River, with yellow trams grinding up the slopes past building fronts covered in painted tiles called azulejos. Porto in the north gave its name both to port wine and to the country. Portugal is a republic with an elected president and parliament, and it joined the European Union in 1986.

Fishing, cork, wine, and visitors drawn by sunshine and surf shape much of the economy.
landAndNature: The Tagus River cuts Portugal in two. North of it the country is green, hilly, and rainy, rising to the Serra da Estrela, where snow falls and the mainland's highest point reaches 1,993 meters. South of the river the Alentejo spreads into wide, dry plains of wheat, olives, and cork oaks, whose bark is stripped by hand every nine years without harming the tree; Portugal produces about half the world's cork. The Algarve coast in the south is lined with golden cliffs and sea caves. Atlantic storms drive enormous waves onto the beach at Nazaré, among the biggest ever surfed, and offshore the Azores and Madeira rise as volcanic peaks where whales gather.
peopleAndCulture: Fado, meaning fate, is Portugal's own music: a singer and a pear-shaped Portuguese guitar performing songs about saudade, a word for longing after something you may never get back. The food centers on the sea, from sardines grilled on street corners at June festivals to bacalhau, salted cod, which Portuguese cooks say has a different recipe for every day of the year. Pastéis de nata, custard tarts in crackly pastry, were first baked by monks in Lisbon. Most Portuguese are Catholic, and summer nights fill with paper lanterns and pots of basil. Soccer is the national passion, and Cristiano Ronaldo, born in Madeira, became one of the most famous athletes alive.
history: Celtic peoples, Romans, and then Muslim rulers from North Africa each shaped this coast. The kingdom of Portugal emerged in 1139 and reached today's borders by 1249, giving it some of the oldest fixed frontiers in Europe. In the 1400s Portuguese captains pushed farther and farther down Africa: Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, and Pedro Álvares Cabral landed in Brazil in 1500. The empire that followed brought spices and gold, and Portugal became a leading trafficker in the transatlantic slave trade, shipping millions of enslaved Africans to Brazil. An earthquake destroyed Lisbon in 1755. A dictatorship ruled from 1933 until the peaceful Carnation Revolution of 1974, after which Portugal's African colonies became independent.
funFacts: Portugal and Spain agreed in 1494 to split newly encountered lands along a line drawn across the Atlantic, which is why Brazil speaks Portuguese.
Lisbon's Tram 28 still uses wooden carriages from the 1930s to climb streets too narrow and steep for modern trams.
Surfers at Nazaré ride some of the largest waves ever recorded, raised by a deep underwater canyon just offshore.
Bertrand in Lisbon, open since 1732, is recognized as the oldest bookshop in the world still selling books.
Cork oaks are stripped of their bark by hand and then left alone for nine years while a fresh layer grows back.
